Each suggestion names the problem it fixes, the official document or repository evidence behind it, two or more paths you could take, and which path this pass would pick and why.
Priority is an editorial judgement by this pass, not a verified fact. It is shown as a score and labelled as judgement so it is never mistaken for measured data.
Every suggestion that cannot be settled without information only you hold links to the exact question that blocks it in the Open questions register.
Effort is estimated in agent-hours of work, not your time: S = under 1 hour, M = 1-4 hours, L = a day or more.

suggestions.title: Confirm the Associates tag is actually inside the three supplied links

If the tag is missing, wrong, or belongs to a different account, every click on this site earns nothing, and nothing on the site would reveal it.

Program Policies, section 2(b): the tag must appear as a parameter in each link to an Amazon Site
Flag F6, root register

options.label: A. Open each link while signed in to Associates Central and watch the click register

A full amazon.com URL with a visible tag is unambiguous on both section 2(b) and 6(w), and it makes the single most commercially important fact on the site verifiable from the page source.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Critical. Every other improvement on this page is worthless if the clicks do not credit your account.

suggestions.title: Say who wrote each page and how it was made - and stop calling the site 'independent'
suggestions.problem: The site presents itself as 'an independent affiliate publisher' while monetising every product page. 16 CFR 465.6 makes it deceptive for a business to materially misrepresent that a website it controls provides independent reviews or opinions. Separately, the pages do not say that the analysis is documentation-based and machine-assisted, which a reader will assume is hands-on testing unless told otherwise.

evidence.label: 16 CFR 465.6 - company-controlled review websites
16 CFR 255.5 - disclosure of material connections
FTC Endorsement Guides Q&A

options.label: A. Replace 'independent' with a precise, verifiable claim
options.what: 'Every specification on this page is quoted from the manufacturer or the US Code of Federal Regulations. We do not do hands-on testing and we say so on every product page.' Same pride, no misrepresentation.

options.label: B. Add an About page naming the method and the author
options.what: One page: who runs the site, how products are chosen, that AI assists with drafting, how corrections are handled, and how the site earns money. Link it from the footer of every page.

options.label: C. Leave the framing and rely on the disclosure bar
options.what: The Amazon disclosure sentence stays in the bar. The 'independent' claim and the missing method statement stay too.

suggestions.recommendation: A and B together. This is the cheapest trust gain available on the site.
suggestions.why: The current copy is already honest about not testing - it just buries that in the footer instead of carrying it as the site's actual selling point. 'We quote the manual, page and section' is a stronger differentiator than 'independent', which is a word every affiliate site uses and which now carries regulatory weight under 16 CFR 465.6.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Medium-high. The word 'independent' next to affiliate links is the specific fact pattern 465.6 was written for.

suggestions.title: Rebuild the landing page around a buyer's question, not a project audit
suggestions.problem: The current landing page opens with 'Three supplied Amazon links: product identity not yet confirmed'. That is an accurate internal status report and a terrible first impression: a reader arriving from a search engine wants to know which air fryer to buy, not which flag is open. The same content done as editorial, in the annex build

options.label: A. Two doors, one site: 'Buying guide' in front, 'Evidence' behind

options.label: B. Keep one page and move the evidence below the fold

options.label: C. Leave it as an audit dashboard
options.what: Appropriate if the site's only reader is you. It will not earn organic traffic or affiliate revenue.

suggestions.recommendation: A, delivered in B's order if time is short.
suggestions.why: The evidence layer is the site's moat and should be reachable in one click, but it is not the product. A page that opens with 'not yet confirmed' cannot convert a visitor who has no idea what F21 is. This is also the exact complaint that prompted this pass.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: High for traffic and revenue. The content already exists - it is a layout problem, not a writing problem.

suggestions.title: Decide what happens to the eight parallel builds before Google decides for you
suggestions.problem: Nine separate HTML sites for the same three products are published on one domain (root plus research/, s2/, site/, dashboard/, docs/, annex-88769516/, session-3740f69d/, articles/). They disagree on facts a reader would take as settled - the Chefman 6 Qt model differs between builds. Every one is indexable, so search engines can crawl nine versions of the same product review on one host.

evidence.label: Repository, top level - every directory with an index.html
Previous passes page cataloguing the disagreements
Flag F35

options.label: A. Keep them in the repo, remove them from the public web
options.what: Move the eight annexes out of the published tree (or serve them with a noindex meta tag and drop them from the sitemap). The repository keeps every session's evidence; visitors and crawlers see one site.

options.label: C. Delete the annexes
options.what: Loses eight sessions of evidence and the record of how the facts converged.

suggestions.recommendation: A. The evidence survives in git history and in the repository; the duplicate-content risk to the one site that matters does not survive at all.
suggestions.why: Search engines do not care that nine builds were produced by nine agents in good faith. They care that nine pages make the same or contradictory claims on one host. Option A keeps the audit trail that makes this project unusual while giving the public site a single, unambiguous identity.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Medium. Diluted crawl budget and a real chance the wrong build ranks.

suggestions.title: Publish no Amazon price or rating unless you hold Creators API access - and know which one you are choosing

But it leaves a comparison table with a 'not displayed' column, which is a weaker buying aid than readers expect.

Creators API / PA-API 5 deprecation notice
Article explaining the policy to readers

options.label: B. Apply for Creators API and render price and rating from it
options.what: Unlocks section 2(b) and 6(t) properly, including star ratings. Requires an approved Associates account, API credentials, and a small server - the site is currently static.

options.label: C. Keep the current 'not displayed' column
options.what: Fully compliant and honest, but the comparison table stays materially less useful than a competitor's.

suggestions.recommendation: A now, B only if the account is approved and you want ratings.

Option B is the real prize - ratings are what most buyers scan - but it needs credentials this session does not have and a host that can keep a secret, which a static GitHub Pages site cannot.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Medium for conversion. Do not fix it by scraping - that breaches section 2(b) and the IP License at once.

suggestions.title: Do not build price tracking or price alerts, whatever the brief asks for
suggestions.problem: The brief asks for a platform that 'analyzes pricing' and 'continuously optimizes campaigns'. evidence.label: Program Policies, section 6(y)
Platform blueprint page, guardrails section

options.label: A. Write the prohibition into the build as a failing test
options.what: A CI check that fails if a price-history, price-alert or chart component ever appears in a generated page or a data file. The rule then cannot be broken by accident in a later pass.

options.label: B. Document it and rely on reviewers
options.what: A note in the platform page. Costs nothing and fails the first time an enthusiastic session does not read it.

options.label: C. Request Amazon's written agreement
options.what: Section 6(y) says 'unless otherwise agreed by Amazon', so a written exception is theoretically available. Realistically not granted to a new account.

suggestions.recommendation: A. Make the policy executable.
suggestions.why: This repository already proves the technique works: build.py refuses to publish a spec row that has a value but no source. The same mechanism should refuse to publish a price-history feature. A policy that lives only in prose gets broken by the next well-meaning pass.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: High. Price tracking is the most commonly requested affiliate feature and the most clearly prohibited one here.

Current measurement plan and deployment gate
GitHub Pages static hosting documentation

options.label: C. Leave the site without on-page analytics
options.what: Use only authorized Amazon reporting when available; query demand remains a Search Console action.

suggestions.why: The code is ready for a deployment review, not for live collection. Associates reports are the authority for affiliate clicks and orders; the local endpoint can add page-level context only after it is actually hosted and disclosed.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Medium. Without measurement, every content decision stays a guess.

suggestions.title: Turn the source-linked articles into a cluster with one job each

Without a deliberate map, the articles that follow will overlap the same way.

Platform blueprint, content engine section
data/articles.json - every article and its sources

options.what: Assign each existing article exactly one search intent (informational, comparison, or transactional). Publish the map. New articles may only target an unclaimed intent. Two articles on one query is a build failure.

options.label: B. Let the articles grow organically
options.what: Publish whatever seems interesting and let search sort it out.

options.label: C. Collapse to three long guides
options.what: One buying guide, one comparison, one product page per SKU. Fewer, deeper pages.

suggestions.recommendation: A, keeping every published article. They are too good to delete and too overlapping to keep growing unchecked.
suggestions.why: The existing title of one article - 'What 450F actually means' - is exactly the kind of specific, answerable question that earns a link and a ranking. The fix is not more articles, it is a rule that stops the ninth from duplicating the fifth.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Low-medium. Costs compounding, not immediate damage.

suggestions.title: Stop presenting the commission rate as unknown where the category is knowable
suggestions.problem: All three products show commission as '- not confirmed -' with two candidate rows, Kitchen 4.50% and All Other Categories 4.00%. That is scrupulously honest, because Amazon publishes rates by category but not which category an ASIN sits in. It is also more cautious than the evidence requires for an air fryer, which Amazon files under Kitchen & Dining - a fact visible in the listing breadcrumb on every one of the three links.

Chefman 6 Qt listing breadcrumb: Home & Kitchen > Kitchen & Dining > Small Appliances > Fryers > Air Fryers

options.label: A. Record the breadcrumb as evidence and show Kitchen 4.50% as the working rate
options.what: Capture the category path Amazon itself displays on each listing, cite it, and show 4.50% as the rate with the breadcrumb as the source. Keep the fallback row visible in a footnote.

options.label: B. Keep both candidate rows until Associates Central confirms the category
options.what: Consulting Reports > Orders, or the Earnings report line item, shows the category Amazon actually applied. Definitive; needs account access.

options.label: C. Leave it as 'not confirmed'
options.what: Defensible, and it costs the reader nothing - but it makes the economics section unusable for deciding whether to invest in this niche.

suggestions.recommendation: B, falling back to A if the account has no earnings history yet.
suggestions.why: A rate at 4.50% versus 4.00% moves the break-even traffic estimate by about 12 percent, which is material to whether the niche is worth the effort. The category is not actually unknowable - Amazon shows it in the breadcrumb and applies it in Reports. Recording 'unknown' when a source exists is a different failure from refusing to guess, and the brief asks for decision-grade information.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Low directly, medium for planning. You cannot size a niche whose unit economics you refuse to compute.

suggestions.title: Check the account against the 180-day qualifying-sale threshold before investing in content
suggestions.problem: Amazon's application review requires qualifying sales within a set window, and an unapproved account earns nothing. The site is currently built as if the account is live. Whether it is, and how much of the window has elapsed, changes the entire plan: an account near the deadline needs conversion work, not more articles.

evidence.label: Associates Central - application review process
Operating Agreement, term and termination

options.label: A. Read the status in Associates Central and record it here
options.what: One line: approved, in review, or closed; and the date the current window started. Everything downstream can then be sequenced against a real deadline.

options.label: B. Assume approved and optimise for revenue
options.what: Proceed as if clicks pay today.

options.label: C. Assume unapproved and optimise for the sale count
options.what: Prioritise the pages most likely to produce a first sale - the highest-intent product review - over broad informational articles.

suggestions.recommendation: A, then C if the answer is 'in review'.
suggestions.why: These two worlds need opposite content. If the account is approved, breadth earns; if it is in review, one high-intent page that produces three sales is worth more than twenty explainers. This session could not read the threshold page's current wording, so the exact figures are flagged unverified rather than restated from memory.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: High if the account is unapproved and the window is running.

A register whose IDs collide cannot be cited reliably, and this repository cites flag IDs from at least six places.

Flag F28 - an earlier collision of the same kind

suggestions.title: Give the site a corrections log, and correct in public
suggestions.problem: This project's most distinctive behaviour is refusing to guess and publishing what it cannot confirm. It has no mechanism for publishing a correction when a previously published value turns out to be wrong - the re-verification page records re-reads, but a reader cannot see 'this number changed on this date and here is why'.

evidence.label: Re-verification ledger - the raw material for a corrections log
Flag F14 - brand-hosted review counts that moved between days
data/reverification.json - the ledger a corrections log would be generated from

options.label: B. Note corrections only in commit messages
options.what: Auditable by a developer, invisible to a reader.

suggestions.recommendation: A. It costs one table and it is the single most credible thing an affiliate site can publish.
suggestions.why: Volatile facts on this site include brand-hosted review counts that changed within 24 hours. A visible corrections log converts the site's biggest weakness - it is not first-hand - into its most defensible claim: you can check everything, including our mistakes.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Low. Opportunity cost.

suggestions.title: Keep automated drafting, but make the claim-check gate the thing you trust
suggestions.problem: The brief asks for content generation at scale. That is achievable here - build.py already refuses to publish an article whose numbers do not appear verbatim in the verified dataset. The risk is the gate being treated as a formality rather than the product, and the IP License forbidding Program Content from being used to train or fine-tune models without approval.

evidence.label: Program Policies, IP License and section 5 - no ML training on Program Content without approval
Program Policies, section 3(c) - you are responsible for the accuracy of all material on your site
Flag F11 - the platform features that need credentials

options.label: A. Generate drafts from manufacturer documents only, and gate every number
options.what: The model may restructure sentences; it may not introduce a value. Every figure must match data/products.json. Program Content never enters the drafting context, which keeps section 5 and the IP License satisfied.

options.label: B. Generate from the Amazon listings too
options.what: Richer input, but listing text is Program Content. Using it to build or fine-tune a model needs Amazon's prior written approval under section 5.

options.label: C. Write everything by hand
options.what: Best quality per page, does not scale, and abandons the brief's automation goal.

suggestions.recommendation: A, with the gate extended to reject any article sentence containing a number that no registered source supports.
suggestions.why: This is already 80 percent built and it is genuinely rare - the guard rejected 18 paraphrased values while the article set was being written. The remaining work is making the gate harder to bypass, not writing more prose.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Medium-high. Scaled content without a numeric gate produces exactly the AI-slop outcome the brief objects to.

Some of these are published; some are not, and the site currently leaves the gaps invisible rather than explained.

evidence.label: Chefman 6 Qt page - specification block
Emeril French Door 360 page - specification block
Full specification register

options.label: A. Add a 'what the manufacturer does not publish' row to each product page
options.what: State plainly which buyer-relevant facts are absent from the official documentation, and that asking support is the only route. Turns a gap into a trust signal at near-zero cost.

options.label: B. Ask the manufacturer for the missing figures
options.what: Chefman and Emeril support can supply dimensions and warranty terms. Authoritative once answered, and answerable in the same email as SG-01 option C.

options.label: C. Buy and measure one unit

suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Low. Pure content quality.

suggestions.title: Decide the domain question before investing in SEO
suggestions.problem: The site is served from kanlerxz87-cyber.github.io/Zone1/. That is a subdirectory of a shared github.io origin, which means its authority is partly shared with every other project on that account and its URLs are ugly to cite. Every inbound link earned today points at a URL you cannot easily migrate later.

evidence.label: Current deployment URL
GitHub Pages custom domain documentation
robots.txt and sitemap.xml generated by build.py, both scoped to the github.io URL

options.label: A. Register a domain and serve Pages from it
options.what: CNAME to GitHub Pages, HTTPS enforced. Roughly the price of a coffee a month. Do it before the first backlink, not after.

options.label: B. Keep github.io
options.what: Free, zero maintenance, and permanent - but weak for search and impossible to move without losing accumulated links.

suggestions.recommendation: A, and do it early enough that the migration is trivial.
suggestions.why: The cost of moving is proportional to the links already pointing at the old address. That number is currently close to zero. Choosing to stay is a decision to be permanently second-class in search; choosing to move later is a decision to lose whatever was earned in the meantime.
suggestions.risk_of_not_doing: Medium, and it compounds in the wrong direction.

suggestions.title: Decide what happens to the eight superseded builds that are still published next to the live site
suggestions.problem: The live site is not one site. This repository publishes 106 HTML pages, and only 27 of them are the maintained build generated by build.py. The rest are seven earlier or parallel builds (dashboard/, annex-88769516/, session-3740f69d/, research/, s2/, site/, docs/), each with its own homepage, its own near-duplicate comparison of the same three products, and in two cases a visible Amazon price. That has two costs. Search: Google's published policy states the presumption that a page matches the overall quality of its domain, and that a review weighs whether 'the same identical or near-identical content appears on multiple other sites' (S30) — nine copies of the same comparison on one origin gives a crawler no signal about which one is maintained, which is why the canonical tag added in this pass (F45) matters. Compliance: Amazon's Program Policies §2(b) permit price display only when Amazon serves the link or the data comes from the Creators/PA API (S2), so any published copy that shows a price is an exposure the maintained build deliberately avoids.

evidence.label: Google Search Central — spam policies (scaled content abuse, site reputation policy, link qualification)
Google Search Central — qualify your outbound links to Google
Amazon Associates Program Policies (price and review display limits, §2(b), §6(t))
The published site and its sitemap (27 canonical URLs)
Flag register rows F44 and F45

options.label: A. Keep the parallel builds, but make the canonical build unambiguous
options.what: Keep every older build published for auditability, since several are cited as evidence by later flags, and rely on the canonical tags added this pass plus a clear link from previous-passes.html. Lowest effort, keeps the audit trail intact, and leaves the duplicate-content risk in place.

options.label: B. Demote the superseded builds out of search without deleting them
options.what: Add a noindex robots meta to each annex build's pages, so the evidence stays online and reachable but stops competing with the maintained site. Needs a one-line change in each annex's own generator, so it is a cross-session change and must be logged on the task board rather than made unilaterally. Removes the duplicate-content risk while preserving every citation.

options.label: C. Remove the duplicate pages and keep only their evidence files
options.what: Delete the HTML of the superseded builds and keep the JSON, Markdown and evidence files they produced, repointing flags that link to them at the repository instead of a live page. suggestions.title: Decide what the AI agent in the brief is allowed to read, before the pipeline is written
suggestions.problem: The brief asks for an AI platform that "automates product research, identifies trending and high-converting products, analyses pricing, reviews, competition, and commission potential". Read against Amazon's IP License, most of the automatic half of that is contractually closed. Section 1 states that Amazon "will not allow any third party to use Program Content to, directly or indirectly, develop or improve large language or multimodal models, machine learning models or related technology". Section 2(e) forbids accessing Creators API, PA API or Data Feeds "for the purpose of aggregating, analyzing, extracting, or repurposing any Product Advertising Content ... or in the direct training or fine-tuning of a machine learning and/or foundational model" without Amazon's express prior written approval. An Amazon listing's title, price, rating and review count are Program Content. An agent that reads Amazon listings to learn what sells is therefore the exact use the licence names; an agent that reads manufacturers' own product pages and owner's manuals is not. This is a constraint on design, and it is cheapest to honour before the pipeline is written.

paths_intro: A decision queue with this many rows is a backlog, not a decision. The paths below group the suggestions into four coherent pieces of work. Each path is ordered, names what has to be true before it can start, and says plainly what it will not fix. Pick one path, finish it, then pick the next. The grouping is this pass's judgement; the dependencies inside it are not - they are the blocked_by links already recorded on each row.
paths_note: Suggested order: P1, then P3, then P2, then P4. P3 is placed second because the domain and canonical-build decisions are cheap and everything published afterwards inherits them; if you would rather see the site convince a human before it meets a search engine, swap P2 and P3. The order is judgement. The dependencies are not. P5 is independent: it is the reader-facing polish path and can run in parallel with any of the four above.

paths.name: Make it safe to publish
paths.promise: Remove the four things that could make the site wrong or non-compliant the day it goes live.
paths.effort: S (four small steps, roughly an afternoon, mostly reading screens you already have open)
paths.must_be_true_first: Nothing. This path is unblocked, which is why it is first.
paths.delivers: Every product page can name the model it is describing; the tag that earns the commission is confirmed; the account is known to be past the 180-day qualifying-sale threshold before anyone writes for it; and the one feature the brief asked for that Amazon's policies forbid is permanently off the table.
paths.does_not_fix: It changes no word a reader sees. The site will be correct and still unconvincing.
paths.pick_this_if: You intend to point a real domain at this within the month.
paths.why_first: SG-01 and SG-02 are the two rows that gate other rows (SG-06, SG-08, SG-10). Every path below assumes the product identity is settled, because content written against the wrong spec table has to be rewritten, not edited.

paths.name: Make it read like a shop, not an audit
paths.promise: Turn a careful source register into a page a buyer can act on.
paths.effort: M (a day or two of writing and one round of design)
paths.must_be_true_first: Path 1, or at least SG-01 - the landing page cannot be rebuilt around a buyer's question while the answer to 'which model is this?' is still blank.
paths.delivers: A landing page that opens with the reader's decision instead of the project's provenance; a named author and an honest method line; the eight existing articles given one job each instead of overlapping; the two facts a buyer actually asks for added to each product page; and a visual layer, licensed before it is published rather than after.
paths.does_not_fix: Traffic. A better page with no visitors is still a page with no visitors.
paths.pick_this_if: The site already gets some visitors, or you are about to send it to someone.
paths.why_first: Conversion work on an unverified product table converts the wrong product.

paths.name: Make it findable
paths.promise: Give search engines one site to index and a reason to rank it.
paths.effort: M (a decision about the domain, then mechanical work)
paths.must_be_true_first: A decision on Q-07 (one site, one domain) and, for SG-10, an answer to Q-11.
paths.delivers: One canonical site instead of eight parallel builds competing with each other; a domain you control rather than a GitHub Pages subpath; the article cluster pointed at distinct search intents; and the commission rate stated where the category is genuinely knowable.
paths.does_not_fix: Whether the content is worth ranking. It removes the structural reasons it cannot.
paths.pick_this_if: You want organic search traffic, which is the only traffic this model gets for free.
paths.why_first: Eight parallel builds on one domain is the single largest reason a search engine would treat this site as low quality, and it is fixable in an afternoon once the decision is made.

paths.name: Make the machinery trustworthy
paths.promise: Automate the parts that can be automated, and put a gate in front of the parts that cannot.
paths.must_be_true_first: Path 1 for SG-06 (it depends on whether Creators API access exists - Q-05), and Q-08 for SG-08.
paths.delivers: Automated drafting kept, with a claim-check gate as the thing you trust rather than the draft; click and conversion measurement that does not breach the privacy disclosure; a flag register where a row number means one thing; a public corrections log; and a settled position on which catalogue data the site may show.
paths.does_not_fix: Revenue on its own - it makes the other three paths repeatable instead of one-off.
paths.pick_this_if: You plan to add products beyond these three, at which point doing this by hand stops working.
paths.why_first: SG-07 already forbids one automation the brief asked for (price tracking). Automating before the guardrails exist automates the mistakes too.

paths.name: Make it read like a publication
paths.promise: The reader-facing polish path: authorship, navigation, brand, imagery, seasons, and clusters - the changes that make the site feel published rather than generated. It carries the parallel passes rows too (SG-27..SG-30: nav labels, the shipped RSS feed, Search Console, reader capture).
paths.effort: M (mostly small changes in the generator and the nav; the calendar and brand rows need one owner decision each)
paths.must_be_true_first: P1's safety rows (SG-01, SG-02, SG-07, SG-11) should be settled, because polish on top of an unconfirmed product identity polishes the wrong thing. Nothing else blocks this path.
paths.delivers: A site a reader can trust at a glance (bylines, one brand, a shopping-shaped nav), a seasonal content rhythm that ships before the moment, a cluster map the generator maintains, and an automation plan pointed at a live API. P5 now also carries the parallel pass's rows (SG-23..SG-25: imagery licensing, seasonal shipping, one compliant call-to-action). These are exactly the changes the brief's 'polished marketing affiliate website, not AI slop' ask describes.
paths.does_not_fix: It does not settle product identity (Q-01/Q-02), the Associates tag (Q-04), or the domain (Q-07) - those remain owner decisions the polish cannot make.
paths.pick_this_if: You want the site to win readers while the account questions are still open, and you are willing to answer two one-message questions (Q-25 brand, Q-23 publishing decisions) to unblock it.
paths.why_first: Not first - parallel. Unlike P1, nothing here can make the site wrong; it can only make it more or less convincing. It can run alongside any other path.

paths.name: Make the money path real: five links, one tag, one report row
paths.promise: Turn what the owner supplied on 2026-11-17 — two more links and a tracking ID — into a site whose commercial links are attributed on evidence rather than on assumption, and whose product set is a decision instead of an accident.
paths.effort: S (two of the three rows are a browser, a report and five minutes; the third is a reading-and-choosing task)
paths.must_be_true_first: Nothing outside the owner's screens. The intent register, the link-test fields, the tagging contract and the five event definitions are merged and enforced by the build, so this path answers questions rather than waiting on code.
paths.delivers: Every submitted link confirmed or explicitly parked; a tracking ID whose attribution has been observed in the Tracking ID Summary Report rather than inferred from markup; a per-channel sub-tag scheme that needs no infrastructure; and a measurement layer whose status, service and disclosure say the same thing in the same tense.
paths.does_not_fix: It will not produce a conversion figure. Orders come from an authorized first-party report, and the campaign ledger's first row is transcribed by a human or does not exist.
paths.pick_this_if: You intend to earn from this site rather than merely publish it.
paths.why_first: It is the only path where the owner's own action unblocks the largest number of other rows, and the only one whose entire bottleneck is a login this repository will never have.
